title: How to work a woven wheel in cross-stitch
subtitle: The circular rose built on a five-spoke base
excerpt: A woven wheel is a circular raised rose made by weaving thread over and under a five-spoke or seven-spoke base. The spokes sit on the fabric first; then the working thread weaves around them in widening circles until the centre is filled. It appears on floral charts as a rose or full flower motif.
sourceNotes: Woven wheel (also called spider web rose) documented in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, embroidery chapter. Standard surface embellishment in British and continental needlework traditions.

glossaryTerms.definition: A circular surface embellishment made by first working an odd number of straight stitches radiating from a central hole (the spokes), then weaving the working thread over and under alternate spokes in a spiral until the spokes are covered. The result is a raised, textured rose or circular motif.

content.text: A
woven wheel
builds a circular, slightly raised rose on the surface of the fabric. The
cross-stitch fill
and
back-stitch outline
go in first; the woven wheel is worked last, positioned over the fabric surface rather than through it.
Working the wheel
Work five straight stitches radiating from a central hole.

Bring the needle up through the fabric at the centre. Take it down at the edge of where you want the rose to sit, then come back up at the centre for each spoke. Five spokes are the minimum; seven give a more rounded wheel. The spokes must be an odd number so the weaving alternates correctly.
Bring the thread up near the centre between two spokes.
Bring the needle up from the back of the fabric close to the centre hole, between any two adjacent spokes. This is the beginning of the weaving thread.
Weave over and under alternate spokes.

Pass the needle over the nearest spoke and under the next, then over the next and under the one after that. Work in a circle, always in the same direction. Do not pierce the fabric: the weaving thread works entirely over the spoke stitches on the surface.
Pack the weaving tightly toward the centre.
After each circuit, nudge the woven thread toward the centre with the needle tip so the weaving sits packed tightly. Continue weaving until the spoke stitches are completely covered.
Take the needle to the back and end the thread.
When the spokes are covered, push the needle through the fabric between the last spoke and the fabric edge. End the thread on the back as normal.
Thread and size

Two strands give a fuller, more raised rose; one strand gives a flatter wheel. The spokes can be worked in a darker shade and the weaving thread in a lighter one, or all in the same colour. A finished wheel of about eight to ten Aida squares in diameter sits in proportion to most floral chart motifs.
